objectives: Define electric current, potential difference and resistance with units.

blocks.title: Current, p.d., resistance
blocks.md:
- **Current I** = charge flowing per second: $I = \frac{Q}{t}$ (ampere, A; 1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current flows from + to −; the electrons really move the opposite way.
- **Potential difference V** (volt, V) = energy transferred per coulomb: $V = \frac{W}{Q}$.
- **Resistance R** (ohm, Ω) = V ÷ I.

blocks.caption: Ohm's law for a metal at constant temperature

blocks.title: Measuring
blocks.md: An **ammeter** is connected in **series** (in line); a **voltmeter** is connected in **parallel** across the component. **Ohm's law**: for a metallic conductor at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the p.d. (the I-V graph is a straight line through the origin). The resistance of a wire increases with its length and decreases with its cross-sectional area; it also depends on the material.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- A filament lamp does **not** obey Ohm's law: its resistance rises as the filament gets hotter, so its I-V graph curves.
- Never connect an ammeter in parallel: its resistance is very low and it would carry too much current.
- Convert mA to A (÷ 1000) and minutes to seconds.

blocks.caption: A circuit with an ammeter A in series and a voltmeter V in parallel with the resistor R.
blocks.alt: A rectangular circuit with a cell, an ammeter in the top wire, a resistor, and a voltmeter connected across the resistor.

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuits
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Current electricity: charge, current, p.d., resistance, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the rules for current and p.d. in series and parallel circuits.
Calculate the combined resistance of resistors in series and parallel.
Solve circuit problems step by step.
Compare series and parallel wiring in the home.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Series circuit
blocks.md: Components in one loop. The **current is the same** everywhere; the p.d. **adds up** ($V = V_1 + V_2$); the total resistance is $R = R_1 + R_2$. If one component breaks, all stop (old Christmas lights).

blocks.title: Parallel circuit
blocks.md: Components on separate branches. The **p.d. is the same** across each branch; the currents **add up** ($I = I_1 + I_2$); the total resistance is smaller than the smallest branch: $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$ (for two resistors $R = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}$). House lights and sockets are in parallel so each works independently at full voltage.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Parallel: do not add the resistances; the total is **less** than each one.
- After using $1/R$, take the reciprocal to get R.
- Check your answer: the total resistance of two resistors in parallel must be smaller than the smaller one.

blocks.caption: Two resistors, 6 Ω and 3 Ω, in parallel across a 12 V cell.
blocks.alt: A battery connected across two parallel branches, one with a 6 ohm resistor and one with a 3 ohm resistor.

blocks.title: Example 1 — series
blocks.statement: A 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor are in series with a 12 V supply. Find the total resistance, the current and the p.d. across each resistor.
steps: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 A (same through both).
V₁ = IR₁ = 1 × 4 = 4 V and V₂ = 1 × 8 = 8 V; check 4 + 8 = 12 V.
blocks.answer: R = 12 Ω; I = 1 A; 4 V and 8 V

blocks.title: Example 2 — parallel
blocks.statement: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are in parallel across a 12 V supply. Find the total resistance, each branch current and the total current.
steps: I₁ = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A and I₂ = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 A (same p.d. across each).
blocks.answer: R = 2 Ω; 2 A and 4 A; total 6 A

lessons.title: Electrical power, energy and safety at home
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Current electricity: charge, current, p.d., resistance, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use P = VI, P = I²R, E = Pt and the kilowatt-hour.
Calculate the cost of electrical energy.
Describe live, neutral and earth wires and safety precautions.
reviewNotes: Mains voltage taken as 220 V (about 220–240 V in different places); frequency 50 Hz. Check against local practice.
Electricity prices are NOT real: the exercises assume a tariff of 100 FCFA per kWh for practice only. The real tariff varies by consumer category and changes over time.
Plug and wire colour codes are not stated because practice differs between countries.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Power and energy
blocks.md:
- Electrical power: $P = VI$ (watts). With Ohm's law also $P = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$.
- Electrical energy: $E = Pt$ (joules, with P in W and t in s) $= VIt$.
- **Kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour. Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h); 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J. Cost = kWh × price per kWh.

blocks.title: House wiring and safety
blocks.md: Mains has a **live** wire (dangerous voltage), a **neutral** wire (return path) and an **earth** wire (safety, to the metal case). A **fuse** (thin wire that melts) or **circuit breaker** is placed in the **live** wire to cut off the current if it is too high. The fuse rating should be **just above** the normal current of the appliance. The earth wire carries a fault current away so that the case never stays live.

blocks.title: Safety rules
blocks.md:
- Never touch switches or sockets with wet hands; water conducts.
- Do not overload a socket with many appliances (overheating and fire).
- Switches and fuses go in the **live** wire so that the appliance is dead when switched off.
- Replace a blown fuse with one of the **correct** rating, never with wire or foil.

blocks.caption: Simplified wiring: live (L) through a fuse, neutral (N), and earth (E) connected to the metal case.
blocks.alt: An appliance box with a live wire passing through a fuse, a neutral wire and a dashed earth wire joined to the metal case.

blocks.title: Example 2 — cost of energy
